answer:
The bubble-point pressure is about 96 kPa (0.96 bar). Water and n-hexane hardly dissolve in each other, so this mixture is not a single liquid at 60 °C. It splits into two liquid layers, each nearly pure. Each layer pushes its own full vapour pressure, so the bubble point is the sum of the two pure-component vapour pressures. The 50/50 overall composition does not affect the result, as long as both layers are present.

I computed the values with Antoine equations (P in mmHg, T in °C):

| Component | Antoine constants (A, B, C) | P_sat at 60 °C |
|---|---|---|
| n-hexane | 6.87601, 1171.17, 224.41 | 76.4 kPa |
| water | 8.07131, 1730.63, 233.426 | 19.9 kPa |
| **Total** | | **96.3 kPa** |

- **First bubble of vapour:** it contains about 79 mol% hexane (76.4 / 96.3) and 21 mol% water.
- **Raoult's law gives the wrong answer here.** Treating the liquid as one ideal solution gives 0.5 × 76.4 + 0.5 × 19.9 ≈ 48 kPa, about half the correct value. That law only applies to liquids that mix.
- **Boiling at 1 atm:** since 96 kPa is just under 1 atm (101.3 kPa), this water/hexane mixture would boil a little above 60 °C at atmospheric pressure. The known heteroazeotrope boils at about 61.6 °C. I did not compute that temperature; it is quoted from memory.

The 96 kPa result assumes the two liquids do not mix at all. Their real mutual solubilities are tiny, so the true value is very slightly lower; I expect the difference to be well under 1%, but I did not model it. The answer rests only on the Antoine correlations, which agree with published data at 60 °C (water about 19.9 kPa; hexane about 76 kPa). I did not check it against a second method.

# ideal-solution (Raoult) for contrast

print('vapour y_hex',ph/(ph+pw))
